items.text:
**Here's an interesting (but dated) one... from the amazing Substack "Net Interest."**

I had occasion today to look through point and reward economics, and next to central banking or sex trafficking or whatever it must be one of the most despicable industries out there. It's well-known that loyalty cards/rewards schemes are fiat money-printing scams that, at best, saddles the user with a below-mininum wage job (https://stacker.news/items/869415).

...but it's good for the companies running these schemes. (Yea, no shit: the money printing/issuing was always great, and under shitty monetary regime there's an incentive for everyone to become a bank or a bank-like entity #[743123](https://stacker.news/items/743123), https://stacker.news/items/1329539)

It's a typical example where businesses do things **against the interest of their customer** (thus, it's dishonest) *while looking* like they're providing you with extra benefits. Somebody should call Lizzy (Warren!). (Also, it's one area where the European Union, in its infinite overlording wisdom, made a limiting regulation that was *actually good* for us Europooreans! By capping interchange fees, they basically outlawed rewards programs and saved/spared 500 million Europeans the time/necessary effort to play these silly money games.)

***

In the age of card networks and (FX) spreads (https://stacker.news/items/1586158) and costs to merchants, the COST and BENEFITS of these (Ponzi?) schemes become entirely intransparent where everyone, like in democracy, think they might get one over on someone else.

At best, it's a selection-biased gamble where **sophisticated consumers take advantage by optimizing the terms/conditions/value of the whole scheme vs naive consumers** who mistakenly believe they can/will win, while the house (as every properly set-up gamble) wins. The naive consumers will inevitably make some sort of error in their financial behavior (overdrafts, not enough spending, not maximizing rewards, too small fish such that annual fee eats up all other benefits).

The most well-known examples here are

* **bank deposits**: people hold too much cash at low-yielding bank accounts vs what they could/optimally should keep in higher-yielding savings accounts. The difference, while maaaybe sometimes convenient for the customer, end up in aggregate securing a massive windfall (=cheap financing) for the banks
* **life insurance products**: life insurance is usually priced very affordably and attractively for the buyer, which the insurance company isn't doing out of ignorance or stupidity but because they know from experience that some portion of the buyers (accidents, life circumstances changing, or just neglect) will let their policies lapse after having paid for a few years, meaning free money for the company, or worse, sell it back to the company at a great discount (=again, free money)

Here's the conclusion from a Fed paper on the subject from a few years ago:

> regardless of income, sophisticated individuals profit from reward credit cards at the expense of naïve consumers. To probe the underlying mechanisms, we exploit bank-initiated account limit increases at the card level and show that reward cards induce more spending, leaving naïve consumers with higher unpaid balances \[...]
> Naïve consumers might underestimate these payments and incur costs from usage. Sophisticated consumers, in contrast, might rake in the benefits while avoiding the payments and thus profit from usage

Here's the graph they use to display the idea (sorted by FICO scores, but the same point stands)

![](https://m.stacker.news/162147)

*tl;dr*, the area between the curves is larger on the negative side than the positive side, thus a) redistributing from naive to sophisticated, but more importantly b) makes the entire scam profitable to the company to run: What it has to pay the sophisticated winners is less than what they manage to extract from the idiot losers.

## The entire edifice is a combination of beggar-thy-neighbor and race to the bottom, with misperception and money illusion becoming key features.

From our pal Matt Levine in a recent Money Stuff piece

> banks make a lot of their money from depositor inattention: When interest rates go up, bank customers mostly don’t move their money, because it would be a pain, so banks can pay below-market interest rates on their deposits.
> You could have similar worries about life insurance, or annuities, or mortgages: Lots of financial products are built (and priced) based on assumptions about customer inattention.

The strategy is that you intentionally misprice (underprice) your service, banking on the fact that, in aggregate, enough people who opt in for this juicy, nice-looking offers will make enough errors that the few sophisticated customers who take perfect, optimized advantage of the mispricing won't cost the company.

***

ANYWAY, **Marc Rubenstein walks through the logic and economics of loyalty programs** and points(!) to some of the intricate cross-subsidized and legal/economic oddities with these programs:

> A key question in the whole points dynamic is how much partners pay for miles. Avios Group deferred revenue at a rate of 0.88 pence per point on the stock it issued in 2023, its highest rate in many years. The consumer value of points varies widely according to how they are used, but The Points Guy puts the value of Avios at around 1.2 pence per point, so the benefit to the consumer is clear. 
> Because the airline can adjust the redemption rate to encourage the use of rewards in ways that reduce their marginal cost, it is able to offer rewards to card issuers at a discount.2 In this way, reward programs can generate profits for both issuers and airlines while generating loyalty to both, a significant positive sum outcome.

## “By minting points, airline companies are able to lock in substantial cash flows.”

> Online points-monitoring sites posting point “valuation” tables on a regular basis because of course the offers change and of course the issuer of this fake, unusable money manipulate it to their advantage.
> The only problem is that competition has been driving up the rate at which card companies pay rewards. Over the last 12 months, American Express has paid out 1.07% of purchase volume in rewards, up from 0.80% ten years ago. Other card issuers have seen similar reward inflation. Capital One paid out 1.29% of purchase volume in 2022, up from 0.80% in 2013. And Discover paid out 1.43%, up from 0.94%. 
> American Express was initially exempt from the EU rules, so my British Airways co-branded card remained unaffected. In 2018, though, the courts brought Amex into line. Fortunately, American Express agreed to eat the cost. My BA Premium Plus card continues to pay 1.5 Avios points for every £1 spent, equivalent to around 1.8% on the basis of The Points Guy’s 1.2 pence per Avios valuation. I guess I do pay £250 per year for the privilege, and Amex likely bought the points at a steep discount (in particular the batch they acquired in 2020 to help the airline out of a liquidity squeeze).

JUST that gives us a few intransparent economic flows:

* First: The Amex bailout of BA during ‘rona, purchasing made-up points at cheap discount… even if Amex nominally loses \~1.3% per dollar of EU transactions, if what they hand over to the customer in rewards (=made-up BA money) was acquired at well below par, there’s still a profit in it for the card company.
* Second, to recoup the yearly card fee of 250 quid, a user needs to transact just below £14,000 a year, basically most of the discretionary card spending for a normal (Europoorean) person… and that’s not giving you pounds back, but made-up BA money you must do some additional trixing (in their webshops, for air fares, for lounge access or extra luggage etc) to benefit from.

## “there are clear subsidies at play. Someone, somewhere is subsidizing my points habit – no longer the merchant, it is now other BA or Amex customers. Indeed, such subsidies are the most controversial aspect to the model.”

I don't quite understand what this percentage is referring to (a larger share of Amex revenues are going back to users than before...?) but it seems to suggest that there is some sort of competitive pressure to close this rent-seeking gap

items.title: Why Were Victorian Elites so Effective? (Works in Progress Magazine, Sam Hughes)
items.text:
## Amazing (long) read, highly recommend

I like Works in Progress. *A lot*. It's a serious outlet for long-form journalism, and it (usually!) features writers whose minds are oriented correctly toward the future. (its editor-in-chief lost his mind during 'rona, so I've stayed away from reading/subscribing or even attempting to contribute... *but I'm often very tempted*)

![](https://m.stacker.news/160670)

## What's the Key For Success?

Work hard, long hours, education, 5am, cold plunges, diversity, pay your politicians well to avoid corruption *blah-blah*?

No, no:

> The elites of Victorian Britain operated differently. Their schools and universities were not terribly academic and had very little STEM. As adults, **they got up late, drank a lot, and spent a remarkable share of their waking hours partying.** They loved feasting, sports, holidays, dancing, and dressing up. Contrary to their stodgy reputation, they were probably a lot of fun.

> the elites of nineteenth-century Britain were, by their own lights, extremely successful. For much of the century, Britain was the richest country on Earth. Its companies dominated global commerce, industry and finance.

## In Defence of Debauchery

![](https://m.stacker.news/160674)

* **SCHOOLING:** while strict (early age, regulated times, single-sex away from family, corporal punishment), the values the English Victorian elite cultivated at boarding school were remarkably progressive: loyalty, internationalism, studies of the arts -- Latin and Ancient Greek --

Amazing:

> There was **resistance to the teaching of science, not because Victorians were hostile to science** in principle, but because they thought it **irrelevant to the kind of moral and cultural formation** that a school for gentlemen was supposed to provide.
> (By contrast, girls were not usually taught classics, meaning that, rather surprisingly, affluent Victorian girls generally followed a more modern curriculum than their brothers.)

While not obviously successful, it cultivated valuable skills:

> ...The most that can be said for Victorians’ classical education is perhaps that, like schooling in any difficult subject, it trained students in self-discipline, memorization, and applying rules.

And *this* we could definitely learn from today:

> Under such circumstances, it is perhaps unsurprising that the share of time spent in the classroom was relatively modest. At Rugby School, weeks were divided into three ‘full days’, three ‘half days’, and Sunday. On a full day, students spent about five hours in the classroom, compared with maybe two hours on a half day.  \[AND, importantly:] They also tended to be shorter than those of contemporary elite schools in France, Germany, or Italy, where the curriculum was normally more academically rigorous.

## "Victorians thought extremely highly of sports, believing that they instilled team spirit and endurance, fostered mutual loyalty, channeled energy and competitiveness, and taught men how to win and lose graciously."

One Loretto School headmaster described the school's priorities: **1) character, 2) physique,** 3) intelligence, 4) manners, 5) information. First time *brawns > brains, eh*

* **UNIVERSITIES**: Not much studying, plenty of "teambuilding"

I found *this* observation interesting:

![](https://m.stacker.news/160677)

> Oxbridge tutors believed overwhelmingly that the purpose of an undergraduate degree was not training for work nor even preparation for academic research, but rather a general moral and intellectual formation that would fit students for any professional role they might later pursue.

also:

> Fellowships were opened up to laymen in the later decades of the century, but **Oxford and Cambridge did not become world-leading research institutions until they were transformed by German scholars fleeing Nazism in the 1930s.** The dominance of Oxbridge in British culture was unusual: these institutions educated a much larger share of the elite than was the case for any two institutions in any other country

Fuck, these peeps just had *great* lives. (In some respects, Oxford life these days is very similar!)

![](https://m.stacker.news/160679)

* **ADULTHOOD**: Busy-busy-fucking busy bee... but not in the way you think

## "One virtue that upper-class Victorian education signally failed to inculcate was early rising. Although Victorian schoolboys and university students got up fairly early for chapel, the day of an upper-class Victorian adult started late."

Fuck *yeah!* Den loves victory https://stacker.news/items/1590741

The great statesmen and prime ministers back then "breakfasted at 9 am" or hosted a "social breakfast starting at 10.30 am (claret was served), continuing till about noon." **A-M-A-Z-I-N-G**

Also, not that different from today (minus the frock)

> general, however, Britain’s elites were slow to suburbanize, and in 1914 most still lived in centrally located row houses and walked to work. Every day a great herd of frock-coated men emerged from Belgravia and Mayfair and poured through Covent Garden to their offices in Parliament, Whitehall, the Inns of Court, and the City.

If you've noticed the drinking *at every goddamn meal*, you're not alone. It's pretty disturbing, an entire nation run by high-functioning alcoholics.

> The Victorians loved drinking and drank a lot by modern standards. Men drank more than women, but women drank a good deal too: one conduct guide[noted that](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/12426/pg12426-images.html)‘young ladies seldom drink more than three glasses of wine at dinner but married ladies, professional ladies, and those accustomed to society, and habits of affluence, will habitually take five or even six, whether in their own homes or at the tables of their friends’.

...and the partying, until the wee hours. Plus, for some odd reason Americans call this "Irish exit" (or French goodbye):

![](https://m.stacker.news/160682)

And they were hardly just for entertainment:

> the social events of the Victorian elite were notable for their lack of segregation by age or sex. A Society ball discharged the functions of both a teenage house party and a business networking convention: in fact, it*was* both a teenage house party and a business networking convention. \[...] Unmarried young people (and their unfortunate parents) might go to three or four balls per week, while other Society members would go to one or two. But the other nights were scarcely less busy. Opera, theatre and concerts were important, especially opening or gala nights.

Fuck, dudes kept busy.

> An MP might miss dinner for a late sitting of Parliament, but still drop into a soirée at 10.30pm, turn up to a supper party at 11.45pm, and then arrive at a ball at 1am. From February to July, the Victorian upper class led a remarkably nocturnal existence, with bedtimes in the small hours and the mornings something of a write-off.

## "All else being equal, rich and powerful Victorians must have been less productive for spending four hours a day in the office rather than twelve. But the creation of a single ruling *Gemeinschaft* may have had compensatory advantages."

Domestic and international (geo)political implications:

> This obviously had advantages for Britain. The elites of the American South had a very different identity to those of the North, and ultimately led the country into civil war. Spain, Italy and France suffered from incessant conflicts between urban bourgeois and rural nobility. Germany was riven with strife along geographical, religious, and class lines. **Some of these tensions existed in Britain, but except in Ireland, the elite finessed them peacefully.**

## "Would modern societies work better if their local and national government were conducted by a tight-knit community of extremely rich and successful people?"

The author thinks not... but a kid can dream, longing as we do for the best moment in (modern) Western civilization: the Victorian era.

items.text:
I have been building a bitcoin block explorer and I feel it's good enough to show:

[https://openbitcoin.com](https://openbitcoin.com)

The site runs its own hardware, bitcoin node and address index. No third-party blockchain API used.

Inside the site:

- Explorer: blocks, transactions and addresses at root-level URLs. (very important, a feature I always wanted with other explorers, a quick easy way to query an address) For example you can type openbitcoin.com/block_number_here or openbitcoin.com/txid_here or openbitcoin.com/address_here to load the page instantly without visiting the site to use the search bar :)

- Node census (openbitcoin.com/nodes): reachable nodes counted by my own P2P crawler, 8,958 nodes from 92 countries last run.

- Rich list (openbitcoin.com/rich-list): top 10,000 addresses and balance distributions.

- Prices: spot price as a median of three exchanges, with a quick conversion tool on the front page.

- Tools: fee calculator, address validator, message verifier, QR generator, and key tools built to be downloaded and run offline.

- Guides: on confirmations, UTXOs, self-custody, stuck transactions and more. Newbie friendly.

- Games (openbitcoin.com/games): three arcade games built on real bitcoin mechanics, stack blocks, clear a mempool backlog, and a slot machine that plays the actual odds of guessing a private key.

The website is open source. What stays private is my server's operational layer.

Would appreciate any feedback, happy to contribute to the community.

items.title: Bitcoin Lightning's security fixes still missing from 71% of flagged nodes
items.text:
### New research reveals widespread delays in patch adoption as public vulnerability warnings fail to accelerate software upgrades.

![](https://m.stacker.news/164574)


## Quick Take

|---|---|---|
|**01**71% of Bitcoin Lightning nodes flagged in an August security disclosure remained on affected software lines in October. | **02**Fixes had been available for more than a year, exposing persistent delays in securing Bitcoin's payment infrastructure. | **03**Security warnings failed to trigger a measurable acceleration in upgrades, raising questions about how operators can be pushed to patch. |

Nearly three-quarters of public [Bitcoin](https://cryptoslate.com/coins/bitcoin/) Lightning nodes identified as exposed in August remained on affected software lines in October.

An [Oct. 21 study](https://cryptoslate.com/bitcoin-lightning-developers-sound-alarm-over-security-flaws-as-second-patch-lands-in-five-days/) found that 71% of a group of 550 public LND nodes flagged during an Aug. 11 security disclosure were still operating on affected software release lines as of Oct. 13.

Only about 10% had upgraded during that period, while 108 nodes were no longer classified as live. The findings suggest that security fixes are reaching some Lightning operators well after their release dates.

The delays are particularly striking because patches for six vulnerabilities covered by the August disclosures had been available since LND version 0.19.0, released 446 days before the public warning.

LND is one of the software implementations used to operate nodes on [Bitcoin's Lightning Network,](https://cryptoslate.com/bitcoin-lightning-developers-sound-alarm-over-security-flaws-as-second-patch-lands-in-five-days/) which processes payments outside the blockchain's main transaction layer.

items.title: In Search of Freedom: Life, Death, and Sovereignty in the Himalaya
items.text:
![](https://m.stacker.news/164458)

*I’m sitting in a dusty hotel room in Kathmandu, attempting to call a Spanish airline about my missing luggage.*
*“We’ll have to email our ground staff contractor,” they say.*
*I try to protest. “My trek starts tomorrow!”*
*“Please check your email later today, sir.”*
*I listen to the click of the agent hanging up the phone.*

The hotel is nestled precisely in the middle of Thamel, the tourist district with its colourful flags, rooftop gardens, and too-narrow streets. There is plenty to do in the capital, but after three days of chasing my lost bag in a Kafkaesque system of virtual shrugs and missed callbacks, my energy wanes. I am trapped in the antipresent, unable to visit any tourist attractions, only capable of reconnecting to the hotel WiFi to refresh my emails for the 800th time in the hope of news. With nothing but time, I feel utterly trapped.

During a 2018 volunteering trip to Nepal, I waited for my opportunity to walk the Annapurna Circuit: a two-week hiking route crossing high paths and winding through tiny Buddhist villages. Instead, I got a call to fly back to the UK. My father had been diagnosed with bowel cancer, and it was terminal. He was the one who introduced me to hiking, taught me to be patient when faced with another false peak, to understand the swirling patterns of clouds, to clean my kit, to be prepared for sudden change, to appreciate in the silence of the wilderness, to be present. Near the end, we talked a lot about hiking.

“When you see a mountain,” he said, “think of me.”
I can’t remember what I said in return.

It took eight years to get back to Nepal — grief, travel, COVID, relocation, work, money, rule changes, and procrastination saw to that. After all my posturing about being an advocate for freedom, living my life exactly how I wanted, my fear of closure held me back. I wouldn’t gain perspective until I’d seen those mountains again.

***

![](https://m.stacker.news/164459)

*Finally, after another two-day delay, I take the first steps of my 18-day trek. The Manang Valley bathes in bright sunlight. We pass apple orchards and fields of buckwheat as we climb to Lower Pisang, but after nearly a week stuck in the hotel, I feel like I could run up the path for hours. I’m not doing this alone; there are ten in my group — other travellers looking for answers in the hills. We get to know each other in the brief moments when we’re not gasping for breath in the thinning air.*

That night, I fire up my Kindle and read [*The Ones Who Walk Away From Omelas*](https://shsdavisapes.pbworks.com/f/Omelas.pdf). It’s one of my all-time favourites, a short story that’s more of a thought experiment. Ursula Le Guin presents a Utopian society of harmony, peace, and joy. In Omelas, life is wonderful for every resident except one: a miserable child, suffering alone in a dungeon. Most residents can ignore the one person whose incarceration guarantees their joy and freedom, but the few who can’t leave the citadel forever.

Maybe it’s hubris, but I’ve always considered myself one of those who ‘walk away’. I’ve been willing to give up convenience to claw back some of the sovereignty I’d lost through a corporate job and living in a mediocre London suburb. And here I was on a legendary remote hiking route, perhaps not scaling peaks, but at least challenging myself, climbing higher than I’ve ever been.

***

![](https://m.stacker.news/164462)

*The nights are cold at 4000m above sea level, and my wardrobe is more suited to the Spanish summer than sub-zero temperatures. As we hike farther up, across metal suspension bridges and past well-insulated herds of yaks, I wear my father’s old gear — a down vest and the bright red* *waterproof. It’s not a homage; it’s purely practical. Still, it gives me some kind of connection.*

I feel him silently judging me for walking the ‘tourist trail’. He always had to plan the route and bring every bit of kit himself, while a Nepalese porter carries my luggage strapped directly to their forehead. He would also have loved seeing the world’s highest peaks up close and listening to the guides' explanations of the dangers, the routes, the climbers. We all live the battle of comfort vs sovereignty.

The ‘tea house’ hotels in the Manang valley have a few more mod cons than expected. Some even have hot showers. But today, the power for the whole village is out. As the sun sets, my roommate and I read by the light of our headtorches.

Before the trip, I’d just finished reading *The Gulag Archipelago*, Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn’s brutal account of the anti-freedoms of Communist Russia. That night, I search for a quote that jumped off the page when I read it: ‘All those years in our cells and our huts, the state’s electricity had seared our souls, and now, darkness was bliss.’ Sometimes, our only freedom comes through stoic minimalism and absence. I turned off my reading light and listened to the darkness.

***

![](https://m.stacker.news/164463)

*I’m in bed with a worsening cold. The lack of doctors and pharmacies doesn’t seem so quaint when you are coughing up your lungs. The 5,416m Thorong La Pass plays on my mind, and I struggle to sleep. It’s not just me; another member of the group has a virus, and most of the others are blowing their runny noses in the dry mountain air. We take each day slowly, climbing 500m in altitude, and putting one foot in front of the other. There aren’t any other options: turning back involves walking too, and I don’t like going backwards.*

By this point, we’ve walked 80km or so. [Karl Bushby](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq8rz38jr50go) has just finished walking 50,000km after circumnavigating the globe by foot. I watched a video on his trip just before setting off on mine, and I was most impressed by the fact he had no desire to break records, no charity campaign, no press team. “Every fibre of my being,” he says, “every day, has been what I'm doing right now.”

Along the way, between icy paths and sneezes, I hit upon the idea that walking is trustless. That’s why it is so freeing to Karl Bushby and to all of us. You don’t rely on anyone or anything else. It is the rhythm of taking one step at a time. Sometimes things go as expected; sometimes they don't. But freedom is not about control. It depends on adapting to your surroundings and being in sync with the path. Each day, the tea houses serve another group of foreigners. Monks in the small temples perform another ceremony, another meditation. The kitchens produce another hundred plates of dal bhat, accompanied by ginger tea for the sniffling guests. The sun rises over snowy peaks again.

One of the guys in our group walked to Everest Base Camp more than 20 years ago. Things were quite primitive back then. He told me the soundtrack of those two weeks was the constant *thunk* of cattle bells. That was his rhythm, his surroundings. He bought a heavy metal bell in a Kathmandu market at the end of his trip and still displays it proudly in his New Jersey house.

***

![](https://m.stacker.news/164464)

*It’s 4 am and -15℃ on the day we climb over the pass and down the other side. Lines of headtorches light the steep path up, and the snow crunches under boots fitted with temporary metal spikes. The path ahead is backed up because a girl from another group has fainted. Her partner attempts to carry her up on piggyback, but stops after just a few steps.*

*As we wait for the last members of our party to arrive, we hop from foot to foot to keep warm. Frank, a German realtor who lives in Cape Town, excitedly tells us he has the WiFi password for a teahouse we’ve just passed. ‘Who cares?’ I think. ‘You’ve flown all the way here to cross this pass, and you’ve gotten up in the dark to do it. Why do you need WiFi?’*

Later, after the girl who collapsed has passed us riding on a yak, after we’ve taken our photos at the top, and after we’ve descended to 3,800 meters and bathed in the sun of the afternoon, I reflect on Frank and his need for WiFi passwords. Yes, we are all plugged into our digital worlds, but if you can’t spend a few hours away from it, are you really free at all?

I think about the amount of time I spent that day completely disconnected, staring at the contrast of birds of prey crossing white peaks and soaring up into a blue sky. Why do we struggle to think beyond the next unit of time? The next breath, photo, coffee break, the next day, the next WiFi access point. Why do we need to extract immediate value from our physical world?

I can’t always rein in my differences from the group. Not everyone has waited eight long years to reconnect with their father by climbing a Nepalese mountain. This is every fibre of my being, not just a social media photo op. My father would have loved to build a homestead, to fix machines, grow cattle, and walk the land, but he chose a secure life so his children could do that.

The next days we pass through small towns celebrating *Dashain* — a time for families, giving thanks, and taking stock. We stay with a local family and experience life in a small town; while we eat set meals and walk to a strict schedule, it feels like all the Nepalis around us are making their own choices.

We watch old ladies harvesting millet and corn. Heavy machinery continues to shift the earth of roads and riverbanks affected by landslides. We see new entrepreneurs opening restaurants, tea houses, and local stores. I speak to Ram, one of our guides, who is working through the festival period to put his kids through college in Japan. Everyone must hustle to improve their lot because saving in Rupees is futile. Even with remittances from those working abroad, Nepal is constantly playing catch-up. Everyone is building a better life here; no one expects it to be easy.

***

![](https://m.stacker.news/164466)

*My final day is spent in Kathmandu. A few of us travel to Durbar Square to see the world’s only living goddess. The Kumari is a young girl selected from a northern village. There are strict physical and mental tests as well as a birthdate that matches specific astrological criteria. She is taken from her parents to live in an opulent palace, where her feet may never touch the ground below. If she sheds a drop of blood, she is cast out into the realm of the mortals and is replaced by a new Kumari. Hindus and Buddhists alike come to see her, hoping to be blessed by one of her three daily appearances at her palace window. The current Kumari is just three years old. After waiting an hour for her to appear, I feel like her nervous little wave is an anticlimax. The crowd still gasps.*

Later, it hits me that she is the living embodiment of the child in *The Ones Who Walk Away from Omelas*. Instead of being tortured or in pain, she is doted on. She has expensive gowns, extravagant makeup, a team of handlers, tutors, and adoring fans, but she is cursed. Her childhood is stolen, and she is imprisoned to bring others luck, joy, and religious harmony. She cannot play, shout, hide, misbehave, cry, laugh, or neglect her duties. She cannot walk where she pleases. To tourists, the Kumari is a sweet anomaly, a curious tradition. To Nepalis, she is a living goddess. Almost everyone is happy with this arrangement.

![](https://m.stacker.news/164460)

I went to Nepal to reconnect with emotions I had long since buried. Curiously, I saw glimpses of freedom instead of apparitions of my father. Sometimes I saw them in the hawks cruising high above, sometimes in the industrious lives of locals, and sometimes in the restrictions of those trapped in digital worlds or religious constructs.

If there is one thing I learned on this journey across the Annapurna mountains, it is that freedom is gained one step at a time. You have to know which direction you are heading, and you must understand what you are leaving behind.

items.title: Why Milei's Chainsaw Revolution Required Restraint
items.text:
> **Critics are divided as Javier Milei takes gradual, constrained steps toward the radical free market he campaigned on.**
>
> In December 2023, as the sound of a chainsaw echoed through Buenos Aires, Javier Milei swept into the Casa Rosada, and pro-market Austrian School economists cheered his victory. Nearly three years later, many libertarians are disappointed. They keep asking themselves: Did they vote for [Rothbard](https://mises.org/profile/murray-n-rothbard), only to get another central planner?
>
> He campaigned on a platform that was not merely reformist but explicitly abolitionist. He promised to end the Central Bank, dollarize the economy, and rein in the interventionist state. The Central Bank of Argentina (BCRA) still opens its doors every morning. The government did not [lift restrictions](https://www.elibrary.imf.org/view/journals/002/2025/219/article-A001-en.xml) on moving foreign currencies until April 2025. To an orthodox libertarian, all of this might still look like central planning.
>
> That criticism has divided free-market thinkers, including Austrian economists. Hans-Hermann Hoppe, for example, has criticized Milei for not acting radically enough. [Milei responded sharply in an interview](https://x.com/LibertarianDuty/status/1867202040742522933) and accused Hoppe of lacking sufficient knowledge of monetary economics. Milei argued that the demands for immediate change ignore important risks, such as hyperinflation.
>
> Milei believes that poorly timed good policy can lead to the worst outcome. He believes that the path to a free market must begin with ending persistent budget deficits, not lifting capital controls. He hopes this approach will advance his political agenda while limiting political tensions and inflation risk.
>
> Milei’s background as a macroeconomist explains his thinking. In this sense, his approach is technocratic because he prioritizes the economic conditions needed to achieve his free-market goals, even if that requires more nuance than his ideological promises.
>

items.title: The Genesis Code, Epilogue: What's Actually There
items.text:
*Harold*

On Saturday mornings, I walk to school.

It's a mile and a half from my room above the dry cleaner to Paperton Central. I used to drive it, back when I taught there, back when I had a car and somewhere I had to be by 7:40. Now I walk it, because I have time, and because there's so much to see.

This morning it was spring. The real kind, the kind that smells like cut grass and wet dirt and somebody's lilacs. The sun came up over the river while I was crossing the Fifth Street bridge, and the whole town turned gold, and I stopped right there in the middle of the sidewalk like a tourist and just looked at it.

I've lived in Paperton my whole life. I'd never once stopped on that bridge.

\* \* \*

Main Street is waking up early these days. Everyone has somewhere they *want* to be.

The old shoe store is a bakery now. A woman named Rita runs it. She did insurance billing for twenty-two years, in a cubicle with no window, and dreamed about bread the whole time. Now she's up at four every morning with flour to her elbows, and the line goes out the door by six, and she sings while she works. Badly. Loudly. Nobody minds.

I bought a loaf of sourdough, still warm, and paid for it with a pale green bill. On the front, there's an old man's hand, open, letting go of something. Rita took it without looking at it, the way you take money, and handed me my change and a free cinnamon roll, because she says I look like a man who appreciates a cinnamon roll.

She's right. She has no idea she's holding my hand in her till. Nobody does. I've spent hundreds of those bills now, all over town, and every single time, it makes me grin like a fool.

Next door, the pawn shop is a guitar shop. Two doors down, the check-cashing place is a bookstore called *Second Chapter*, run by the same man who used to cash checks there, who says he finally has customers who leave happier than they came in. Across the street, there's a little shop with a hand-painted sign that just says *REPAIRS: ANYTHING*, where a retired machinist fixes toasters and lawnmowers and bicycles for whatever you can pay, and teaches anybody who wants to learn.

Down by the river, two brothers who used to drive forklifts at the distribution center are building wooden boats. They've sold eleven. They waved at me from the dock with their sleeves rolled up and sawdust in their hair, and one of them yelled, "Mr. Horcross! Come see the new one!" They were in my art class in 1994. They both drew boats then, too.

That's the thing I keep noticing. Nobody in Paperton asks "What do you do?" anymore.

They ask, "What are you making?"

\* \* \*

It turns out that when the money holds still, people stop holding their breath.

Nobody's paying interest on anything. Nobody's savings shrink while they sleep. The lights cost almost nothing, because half the basements in town have one of those 1971 batteries now, built down at the old tool-and-die shop by six guys who couldn't be happier arguing about voltage. Medical school is free. Trade school is free. Starting a business means borrowing from your neighbors at zero percent, because zero is the only number allowed.

And so people did the thing they'd always been too scared to do.

They went after it. The bread. The boats. The guitar shop, the nursing degree, the farm, the band, the book they'd been meaning to write for thirty years. Not all of them made it. Some tried three things before one worked. But trying doesn't cost you your house anymore. And a town full of people doing what they love turns out to be the best place I've ever lived.

\* \* \*

Walt was fishing off the end of the old railroad pier, the way he is every morning now. He held up a perch as I went by, very proud, and hollered, "Eighteen months clean, Harold! Doc says there's nothing left to find!"

Walt had cancer for three years. The kind with a bill every month and no end in sight. Then the vaults opened, and out of a plain gray box in Chicago came the Sollen protocol: a treatment from 1986 that teaches the body to find the cancer and finish it, in four visits. Four. Then you go home and go fishing.

The memo clipped to that file has become the most famous sentence of the century. They teach it in schools now. *A cure is sold once. A treatment is sold for life.*

Once people read that, they couldn't unread it. And something changed in how the whole world thinks about getting well. Labs everywhere are racing now, not to manage diseases, but to end them, one after another, and give the answers away. Every month there's news. A cure here. A breakthrough there. My neighbor Ellen, who was in a wheelchair for eleven years, walked to her mailbox last week on her own two feet, on Halverin-9, and the whole street came out and applauded, and she curtsied.

People aren't afraid of the doctor anymore. They're afraid of missing out on their lives, which is a much better thing to be afraid of.

\* \* \*

If the vaults taught the world anything, it's this: an idea locked in a basement helps nobody. So people stopped locking them up.

It's written right into the Charter, on page nine. Anything released to the public stays free, forever. Anyone can use it, change it, improve it, and build on it, so long as they share what they build the same way. The programmers have an old word for that. They call it *copyleft*. Toshi explained it to me once: "Copyright says *mine*. Copyleft says *ours, and keep it that way.*"

And then there are the printers.

There's a 3D printer in every library in Paperton now, and the high school, and the fire station, and the back of the repair shop on Main Street. There's even one in the corner of Room 114. You find a design someone shared, anyone, anywhere in the world, and you print it. A part for your tractor. A pump for your well. A battery casing. A brace for your bad knee. A tiny hand for a little girl who was born without one, printed in her favorite color, purple, at the library on a Tuesday afternoon, while her mother cried and the librarian pretended not to.

The cures work the same way now. A lab in Nairobi improved the Sollen protocol last fall and posted it the same day. A lab in Cleveland improved *that* one in the winter. A grad student in Seoul found a way to make Halverin-9 out of things you can grow. Nobody's hiding anything. Nobody's sitting on anything, waiting for the price to go up. The answers go out into the world as fast as people find them, and the next person picks them up and runs.

And here's the part I love: good ideas get rewarded.

Every shared design, every formula, every invention carries its maker's wallet address, right there at the bottom, like a signature. When something you downloaded helps you, you send a little thanks, in People's Currency, straight to the person who made it. No bank in the middle. No company taking a cut. Just one person saying thank you to another.

A sixteen-year-old in Toledo designed that little printable hand. It's been printed two million times, in a hundred and forty countries. The thank-yous paid for her college, and her mother's house, and a workshop where she's teaching other kids to design hands.

The old system paid people for owning ideas. The new one pays them for sharing.

Turns out sharing works better.

\* \* \*

I hear from the others, now and then.

Toshi sends postcards from Columbus, no return address. The last one said: *The logs are clean. Somebody found the bottle. Turns out it was fixable.* He's teaching a free coding class for kids. He says half of them want to build robots and the other half want to build money, and he teaches every one of them the genesis code.

Marcy runs the town halls in four states, and laughs more than anyone I've ever met.

Dolores lends money at zero percent to young people starting businesses in Youngstown. Her pickle jar sits on her kitchen shelf, empty, next to a picture of her grandson in his graduation gown. She calls me sometimes. She doesn't know who I am. She thinks I'm just a nice old man from Paperton who once sent her a letter. That's true.

Cyrus Vail teaches a night class called *Ethics*. There's a waiting list.

And the robot is everywhere.

People see him at a town hall in Arizona, sitting in the back, listening. On a farm in Iowa, helping with the harvest. At a children's hospital in Detroit, reading out loud. Holding a place in line every November at polling places all over the country. There were more than twenty of him by the end, after all. I like to think all the stories are true.

\* \* \*

Room 114 was full when I got there.

Full. Every table. Kids, mostly, with their parents dropping them off and then staying, because the parents wanted to draw too. A delivery driver who's working on a comic book. A grandmother learning watercolors. The two boat brothers, who came by to show me the drawings for their next hull. And the boy in the Cincinnati Reds T-shirt, nine years old, who draws nothing but robots.

I set an old work glove on the table in the middle of the room and told them to draw it.

The boy drew a robot hand, shiny and perfect, with lightning bolts coming out of the fingers. I sat down beside him.

"That's a great robot hand," I said. "Now look again. Draw what's actually there."

He looked at the glove for a long time. The cracked leather. The hole in the thumb. The one bent finger, like it remembered holding something.

Then he turned his paper over and started again, and what he drew was lopsided and heavy-handed and the thumb was much too big, and it was the most honest thing anyone made in that room all morning. When he held it up, the whole class clapped. He went pink right up to his ears.

Then, in the corner of the page, very small, he added a little robot. Waving.

"Is that allowed?" he asked.

"That," I said, "is the whole point."

\* \* \*

When everyone had gone, I stayed a while. The Saturday sun was pouring in sideways through the big windows, and from down the hall, I could hear a pickup basketball game in the gym, and from outside, somebody's radio playing, and somebody laughing.

I took out a fresh sheet of paper and a pencil.

For most of my life, I drew what was in front of me: the empty storefronts, the shut-down plant, the tired faces at the bar. I drew what was actually there, because that's what you're supposed to do, and because back then, that's all there was.

But what's actually there has changed.

So I drew the bridge in the morning light. Rita with flour to her elbows. Walt holding up his perch. The boat brothers. Ellen at her mailbox. A boy in a Reds shirt, holding up a lopsided glove.

And somewhere, very soft, the way you feel a hand on your shoulder, I felt it.

*We,* it said.

I smiled, and I turned the page.

There's so much left to draw.

---

*The Genesis Code: Block One* by E. G. Gore. That's the whole book, one chapter a day until Election Day. Thank you for reading along, and go vote. 🗳️

The whole book is free at https://eggore.com (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0). Earlier chapters are on my profile.

items.title: Who wore it better? - Political Propaganda in the Buckeye State
items.text:
# Ground Zero

I live in a very purple county in a very purple state. What's that translate to in day to day living? Sooooooo much mail. I would like to share one piece of recent mail that made me laugh from each side of an election. Presumably, they may make you laugh as well.

# The Grand ol' Party

Representing the right side of the aisle, we have an ad that I find kind of silly. It **looks** like propaganda. What's probably most disturbing to me about this is that I can't actually figure out if it's supposed to be silly or not.

![](https://m.stacker.news/163714)

Then I turned it over. This drives me bonkers, and it's increasingly becoming common among political folk. Of course, I'm talking about using an adjective as a noun. "Illegals" cannot be plural because illegal cannot be singular. In the English, you can have illegal cucumber**s** or protractor**s** or even planet**s**, but you can't have illegal**s**.

![](https://m.stacker.news/163723)

It's just nonsensical. The only thing it says to a guy like me, is that the writer doesn't really have a strong handle on the English language, which is ironic, given what I think he's trying to express! A fun follow up question someone should have asked when proofreading this add is whether or not the writer was referring to legal illegals or illegal illegals. I think at that point, he could have clarified that he meant criminals.

# The Eeyores

Let's step to the left and see what's being distributed. To me this one is less fun and games, and far more sinister. My wife literally opened this up and started reading it to the family because it was from the "Center for Voter Information" and clearly looked like it was just listing where candidates stood on the issues. items.title: Reddit is moving to “a logged-in-only experience,” CEO says
items.text:
> Moving to primarily logged-in will ensure our users have the best Reddit experience possible, and can find the content and communities most relevant to them. It is better for our business because we will have more signals for ads targeting, and being logged-in leads to higher engagement generally. It also allows us to protect access to Reddit’s extremely valuable corpus of data, and helps us better adapt to emerging regulations around the world.

Ostensibly, this is because people aren't going to reddit, they're going to their favorite LLM overlord and the LLM is then relying on data scraped in part from reddit. This means search-referral traffic is down. 

> “During October, we have seen that search traffic has dropped by more than 1 million referrals on average per week. If this rate of decline continues, current trends would suggest that total DAUqs [or daily active unique users] could fall in Q4, by a low-double-digit percentage from our current base of 130 million DAUqs,” Huffman wrote.

I believe many people have predicted that the result of widespread use of LLMs would be the building of walls around every platform. X already requires logins to read, reddit seems to be coming soon. It seems like you can still view Instagram and TikTok posts without logging in (although the experience is a little clunky) and Facebook is semi-visible (only public pages can be viewed without login?)

I find this trend unpleasant: the open, public internet has been a source of great joy to me, and seeing it Balkanized like this is sad.

But also I think it is the opposite of what people should be doing: if anything we should be focusing on increasing the cost of posting on the internet, not reading. Or am I wrong about this?

items.title: [Parent Corner] Finding the right activity
items.text:
My daughter started swim lessons this weekend and it was such a breath of fresh air. Up to this point, organized activities have been a real slog, even when she says she enjoys them. Her attention never held and she'd start goofing off and disrupting things for others.

Not so with swimming! As soon as she was in the water with her instructor she was locked-in, appearing to be fully engaged the whole time and having lots of fun. She was still messing around a little bit, but now it came in the flow of the activity. She even complained to us afterwards about the other kid in her lessons not following all the instructions! 

She made meaningful progress, too. Our neighborhood has a pool, so she's spent a lot of time in the water but she never wanted to dunk her head under or try swimming without assistance. She was doing both happily by the end of the lesson and her instructor thinks she's just about ready for the next level.

It's a huge relief for us to know that she *can* cooperate and stay on task for prolonged periods. Now we just need to bridge these skills over to other domains.

If you're struggling to find the right activity for your kid, keep at it. There's no telling what it might be but you'll know it when you see it.

items.title: Who Patches the Lightning Network? Evidence from Release Lines in Gossip
items.text:
### Abstract

> Every implementation of Bitcoin's Lightning payment network disclosed security vulnerabilities in 2026, and every advisory told operators to upgrade. Whether they do has never been measured, because Lightning gossip carries no software version. Matching the feature bits a node announces against the source of every LND, Core Lightning, Eclair and LDK release, we show that gossip reveals a node's release line after all. Where Core Lightning nodes state their version, the inferred line is exact for 132 of 136 node-line pairs. Across 814 daily snapshots of the public graph from 2023 to 2026, the network patches on release and platform schedules, not on disclosures. Half of LND nodes upgrade within 88 days of a release; small nodes and those that skipped releases lag far behind. The three largest upgrade waves came about a day after the Umbrel app store shipped a new LND version. Since June 2025, 17% of LND upgrades came in the 48 hours after a platform release, windows that cover 4.4% of the time. Disclosures, a median 256 days after the fix, moved few operators: of 12 we can test, only Core Lightning's of July 2026 sped up upgrades, and only among nodes one release line behind. Its later call to restart offline was followed mostly by nodes already patched. Two months after Lightning Labs' August 2026 batch, 71% of the LND nodes exposed at disclosure still ran an affected release. For maintainers, the lever on the nodes that lag is the platforms that package their releases.

### Introduction

The Lightning Network is a payment network built on Bitcoin. Its nodes run open-source software and hold their operators’ funds in payment channels, so a flaw in that software can put those funds at risk. Between July and October 2026, every major Lightning implementation disclosed security vulnerabilities. Lightning Labs published ten LND advisories on a single day<sup>\[</sup>[<sup>1</sup>](https://arxiv.org/html/2610.30350v1#bib.bib1)<sup>]</sup> and eight more a month later<sup>\[</sup>[<sup>2</sup>](https://arxiv.org/html/2610.30350v1#bib.bib2)<sup>]</sup>; Core Lightning (CLN) asked operators who could not upgrade to restart their nodes offline<sup>\[</sup>[<sup>3</sup>](https://arxiv.org/html/2610.30350v1#bib.bib3)<sup>]</sup>; Eclair and LDK shipped security releases. Each advisory ends with the same advice: upgrade. Whether operators do, and how fast, decides how long a disclosed vulnerability stays exploitable, and by October CLN’s maintainers reported attacks on unpatched nodes <sup>\[</sup>[<sup>4</sup>](https://arxiv.org/html/2610.30350v1#bib.bib4)<sup>]</sup>. For web servers, browsers and Bitcoin and Ethereum full nodes, how fast operators patch has been measured for two decades<sup>\[</sup>[<sup>5</sup>](https://arxiv.org/html/2610.30350v1#bib.bib5)<sup>, </sup>[<sup>6</sup>](https://arxiv.org/html/2610.30350v1#bib.bib6)<sup>, </sup>[<sup>7</sup>](https://arxiv.org/html/2610.30350v1#bib.bib7)<sup>, </sup>[<sup>8</sup>](https://arxiv.org/html/2610.30350v1#bib.bib8)<sup>, </sup>[<sup>9</sup>](https://arxiv.org/html/2610.30350v1#bib.bib9)<sup>]</sup>. For the Lightning Network it has not, because Lightning gossip carries no software version: earlier studies could tell which implementation a node runs<sup>\[</sup>[<sup>10</sup>](https://arxiv.org/html/2610.30350v1#bib.bib10)<sup>, </sup>[<sup>11</sup>](https://arxiv.org/html/2610.30350v1#bib.bib11)<sup>, </sup>[<sup>12</sup>](https://arxiv.org/html/2610.30350v1#bib.bib12)<sup>]</sup>, not which release.

items.title: Hot Take: Halloween shows the decline of civic society
items.text:
As an American, it strikes me every year that Halloween is pretty much the only widely celebrated public event where people go out in their neighborhoods to socialize and celebrate together.  Not even the 4th of July commands such activity, nor any of the religious holidays.

And yet, it is heavily commercialized, representing a huge subsidy to the sugar industry as people exchange candy in a wide circle, getting back just as much as they gave out, with no real net candy benefit to anyone, and probably net negative health and financial consequences to individual households.

The public displays that people put up on their houses are also getting more and more inappropriate every year, with many seeming to take pride in how scary and realistic they can make their displays look.

It is also a public celebration of make-believe.  Nothing about it is rooted in anything real, or any claim of truth.  In fact, it is explicitly recognized by all involved that everything about it is fake.  In essence, we are celebrating make-believe, and the reason this is the only thing left to celebrate is because the culture has no more shared value or truth claim of any kind.

What say you, stackers?  If SimpleStacker shaking his fist at the wind?  Or is there something to my curmudgeony thoughts?

items.title: Bitcoin Lightning's security fixes still missing from 71% of flagged nodes
items.text:
### New research reveals widespread delays in patch adoption as public vulnerability warnings fail to accelerate software upgrades.

![](https://m.stacker.news/164574)


## Quick Take

|---|---|---|
|**01**71% of Bitcoin Lightning nodes flagged in an August security disclosure remained on affected software lines in October. | **02**Fixes had been available for more than a year, exposing persistent delays in securing Bitcoin's payment infrastructure. | **03**Security warnings failed to trigger a measurable acceleration in upgrades, raising questions about how operators can be pushed to patch. |

Nearly three-quarters of public [Bitcoin](https://cryptoslate.com/coins/bitcoin/) Lightning nodes identified as exposed in August remained on affected software lines in October.

An [Oct. 21 study](https://cryptoslate.com/bitcoin-lightning-developers-sound-alarm-over-security-flaws-as-second-patch-lands-in-five-days/) found that 71% of a group of 550 public LND nodes flagged during an Aug. 11 security disclosure were still operating on affected software release lines as of Oct. 13.

Only about 10% had upgraded during that period, while 108 nodes were no longer classified as live. The findings suggest that security fixes are reaching some Lightning operators well after their release dates.

The delays are particularly striking because patches for six vulnerabilities covered by the August disclosures had been available since LND version 0.19.0, released 446 days before the public warning.

LND is one of the software implementations used to operate nodes on [Bitcoin's Lightning Network,](https://cryptoslate.com/bitcoin-lightning-developers-sound-alarm-over-security-flaws-as-second-patch-lands-in-five-days/) which processes payments outside the blockchain's main transaction layer.

items.title: In Search of Freedom: Life, Death, and Sovereignty in the Himalaya
items.text:
![](https://m.stacker.news/164458)

*I’m sitting in a dusty hotel room in Kathmandu, attempting to call a Spanish airline about my missing luggage.*
*“We’ll have to email our ground staff contractor,” they say.*
*I try to protest. “My trek starts tomorrow!”*
*“Please check your email later today, sir.”*
*I listen to the click of the agent hanging up the phone.*

The hotel is nestled precisely in the middle of Thamel, the tourist district with its colourful flags, rooftop gardens, and too-narrow streets. There is plenty to do in the capital, but after three days of chasing my lost bag in a Kafkaesque system of virtual shrugs and missed callbacks, my energy wanes. I am trapped in the antipresent, unable to visit any tourist attractions, only capable of reconnecting to the hotel WiFi to refresh my emails for the 800th time in the hope of news. With nothing but time, I feel utterly trapped.

During a 2018 volunteering trip to Nepal, I waited for my opportunity to walk the Annapurna Circuit: a two-week hiking route crossing high paths and winding through tiny Buddhist villages. Instead, I got a call to fly back to the UK. My father had been diagnosed with bowel cancer, and it was terminal. He was the one who introduced me to hiking, taught me to be patient when faced with another false peak, to understand the swirling patterns of clouds, to clean my kit, to be prepared for sudden change, to appreciate in the silence of the wilderness, to be present. Near the end, we talked a lot about hiking.

“When you see a mountain,” he said, “think of me.”
I can’t remember what I said in return.

It took eight years to get back to Nepal — grief, travel, COVID, relocation, work, money, rule changes, and procrastination saw to that. After all my posturing about being an advocate for freedom, living my life exactly how I wanted, my fear of closure held me back. I wouldn’t gain perspective until I’d seen those mountains again.

***

![](https://m.stacker.news/164459)

*Finally, after another two-day delay, I take the first steps of my 18-day trek. The Manang Valley bathes in bright sunlight. We pass apple orchards and fields of buckwheat as we climb to Lower Pisang, but after nearly a week stuck in the hotel, I feel like I could run up the path for hours. I’m not doing this alone; there are ten in my group — other travellers looking for answers in the hills. We get to know each other in the brief moments when we’re not gasping for breath in the thinning air.*

That night, I fire up my Kindle and read [*The Ones Who Walk Away From Omelas*](https://shsdavisapes.pbworks.com/f/Omelas.pdf). It’s one of my all-time favourites, a short story that’s more of a thought experiment. Ursula Le Guin presents a Utopian society of harmony, peace, and joy. In Omelas, life is wonderful for every resident except one: a miserable child, suffering alone in a dungeon. Most residents can ignore the one person whose incarceration guarantees their joy and freedom, but the few who can’t leave the citadel forever.

Maybe it’s hubris, but I’ve always considered myself one of those who ‘walk away’. I’ve been willing to give up convenience to claw back some of the sovereignty I’d lost through a corporate job and living in a mediocre London suburb. And here I was on a legendary remote hiking route, perhaps not scaling peaks, but at least challenging myself, climbing higher than I’ve ever been.

***

![](https://m.stacker.news/164462)

*The nights are cold at 4000m above sea level, and my wardrobe is more suited to the Spanish summer than sub-zero temperatures. As we hike farther up, across metal suspension bridges and past well-insulated herds of yaks, I wear my father’s old gear — a down vest and the bright red* *waterproof. It’s not a homage; it’s purely practical. Still, it gives me some kind of connection.*

I feel him silently judging me for walking the ‘tourist trail’. He always had to plan the route and bring every bit of kit himself, while a Nepalese porter carries my luggage strapped directly to their forehead. He would also have loved seeing the world’s highest peaks up close and listening to the guides' explanations of the dangers, the routes, the climbers. We all live the battle of comfort vs sovereignty.

The ‘tea house’ hotels in the Manang valley have a few more mod cons than expected. Some even have hot showers. But today, the power for the whole village is out. As the sun sets, my roommate and I read by the light of our headtorches.

Before the trip, I’d just finished reading *The Gulag Archipelago*, Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn’s brutal account of the anti-freedoms of Communist Russia. That night, I search for a quote that jumped off the page when I read it: ‘All those years in our cells and our huts, the state’s electricity had seared our souls, and now, darkness was bliss.’ Sometimes, our only freedom comes through stoic minimalism and absence. I turned off my reading light and listened to the darkness.

***

![](https://m.stacker.news/164463)

*I’m in bed with a worsening cold. The lack of doctors and pharmacies doesn’t seem so quaint when you are coughing up your lungs. The 5,416m Thorong La Pass plays on my mind, and I struggle to sleep. It’s not just me; another member of the group has a virus, and most of the others are blowing their runny noses in the dry mountain air. We take each day slowly, climbing 500m in altitude, and putting one foot in front of the other. There aren’t any other options: turning back involves walking too, and I don’t like going backwards.*

By this point, we’ve walked 80km or so. [Karl Bushby](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq8rz38jr50go) has just finished walking 50,000km after circumnavigating the globe by foot. I watched a video on his trip just before setting off on mine, and I was most impressed by the fact he had no desire to break records, no charity campaign, no press team. “Every fibre of my being,” he says, “every day, has been what I'm doing right now.”

Along the way, between icy paths and sneezes, I hit upon the idea that walking is trustless. That’s why it is so freeing to Karl Bushby and to all of us. You don’t rely on anyone or anything else. It is the rhythm of taking one step at a time. Sometimes things go as expected; sometimes they don't. But freedom is not about control. It depends on adapting to your surroundings and being in sync with the path. Each day, the tea houses serve another group of foreigners. Monks in the small temples perform another ceremony, another meditation. The kitchens produce another hundred plates of dal bhat, accompanied by ginger tea for the sniffling guests. The sun rises over snowy peaks again.

One of the guys in our group walked to Everest Base Camp more than 20 years ago. Things were quite primitive back then. He told me the soundtrack of those two weeks was the constant *thunk* of cattle bells. That was his rhythm, his surroundings. He bought a heavy metal bell in a Kathmandu market at the end of his trip and still displays it proudly in his New Jersey house.

***

![](https://m.stacker.news/164464)

*It’s 4 am and -15℃ on the day we climb over the pass and down the other side. Lines of headtorches light the steep path up, and the snow crunches under boots fitted with temporary metal spikes. The path ahead is backed up because a girl from another group has fainted. Her partner attempts to carry her up on piggyback, but stops after just a few steps.*

*As we wait for the last members of our party to arrive, we hop from foot to foot to keep warm. Frank, a German realtor who lives in Cape Town, excitedly tells us he has the WiFi password for a teahouse we’ve just passed. ‘Who cares?’ I think. ‘You’ve flown all the way here to cross this pass, and you’ve gotten up in the dark to do it. Why do you need WiFi?’*

Later, after the girl who collapsed has passed us riding on a yak, after we’ve taken our photos at the top, and after we’ve descended to 3,800 meters and bathed in the sun of the afternoon, I reflect on Frank and his need for WiFi passwords. Yes, we are all plugged into our digital worlds, but if you can’t spend a few hours away from it, are you really free at all?

I think about the amount of time I spent that day completely disconnected, staring at the contrast of birds of prey crossing white peaks and soaring up into a blue sky. Why do we struggle to think beyond the next unit of time? The next breath, photo, coffee break, the next day, the next WiFi access point. Why do we need to extract immediate value from our physical world?

I can’t always rein in my differences from the group. Not everyone has waited eight long years to reconnect with their father by climbing a Nepalese mountain. This is every fibre of my being, not just a social media photo op. My father would have loved to build a homestead, to fix machines, grow cattle, and walk the land, but he chose a secure life so his children could do that.

The next days we pass through small towns celebrating *Dashain* — a time for families, giving thanks, and taking stock. We stay with a local family and experience life in a small town; while we eat set meals and walk to a strict schedule, it feels like all the Nepalis around us are making their own choices.

We watch old ladies harvesting millet and corn. Heavy machinery continues to shift the earth of roads and riverbanks affected by landslides. We see new entrepreneurs opening restaurants, tea houses, and local stores. I speak to Ram, one of our guides, who is working through the festival period to put his kids through college in Japan. Everyone must hustle to improve their lot because saving in Rupees is futile. Even with remittances from those working abroad, Nepal is constantly playing catch-up. Everyone is building a better life here; no one expects it to be easy.

***

![](https://m.stacker.news/164466)

*My final day is spent in Kathmandu. A few of us travel to Durbar Square to see the world’s only living goddess. The Kumari is a young girl selected from a northern village. There are strict physical and mental tests as well as a birthdate that matches specific astrological criteria. She is taken from her parents to live in an opulent palace, where her feet may never touch the ground below. If she sheds a drop of blood, she is cast out into the realm of the mortals and is replaced by a new Kumari. Hindus and Buddhists alike come to see her, hoping to be blessed by one of her three daily appearances at her palace window. The current Kumari is just three years old. After waiting an hour for her to appear, I feel like her nervous little wave is an anticlimax. The crowd still gasps.*

Later, it hits me that she is the living embodiment of the child in *The Ones Who Walk Away from Omelas*. Instead of being tortured or in pain, she is doted on. She has expensive gowns, extravagant makeup, a team of handlers, tutors, and adoring fans, but she is cursed. Her childhood is stolen, and she is imprisoned to bring others luck, joy, and religious harmony. She cannot play, shout, hide, misbehave, cry, laugh, or neglect her duties. She cannot walk where she pleases. To tourists, the Kumari is a sweet anomaly, a curious tradition. To Nepalis, she is a living goddess. Almost everyone is happy with this arrangement.

![](https://m.stacker.news/164460)

I went to Nepal to reconnect with emotions I had long since buried. Curiously, I saw glimpses of freedom instead of apparitions of my father. Sometimes I saw them in the hawks cruising high above, sometimes in the industrious lives of locals, and sometimes in the restrictions of those trapped in digital worlds or religious constructs.

If there is one thing I learned on this journey across the Annapurna mountains, it is that freedom is gained one step at a time. You have to know which direction you are heading, and you must understand what you are leaving behind.

items.title: Why Milei's Chainsaw Revolution Required Restraint
items.text:
> **Critics are divided as Javier Milei takes gradual, constrained steps toward the radical free market he campaigned on.**
>
> In December 2023, as the sound of a chainsaw echoed through Buenos Aires, Javier Milei swept into the Casa Rosada, and pro-market Austrian School economists cheered his victory. Nearly three years later, many libertarians are disappointed. They keep asking themselves: Did they vote for [Rothbard](https://mises.org/profile/murray-n-rothbard), only to get another central planner?
>
> He campaigned on a platform that was not merely reformist but explicitly abolitionist. He promised to end the Central Bank, dollarize the economy, and rein in the interventionist state. The Central Bank of Argentina (BCRA) still opens its doors every morning. The government did not [lift restrictions](https://www.elibrary.imf.org/view/journals/002/2025/219/article-A001-en.xml) on moving foreign currencies until April 2025. To an orthodox libertarian, all of this might still look like central planning.
>
> That criticism has divided free-market thinkers, including Austrian economists. Hans-Hermann Hoppe, for example, has criticized Milei for not acting radically enough. [Milei responded sharply in an interview](https://x.com/LibertarianDuty/status/1867202040742522933) and accused Hoppe of lacking sufficient knowledge of monetary economics. Milei argued that the demands for immediate change ignore important risks, such as hyperinflation.
>
> Milei believes that poorly timed good policy can lead to the worst outcome. He believes that the path to a free market must begin with ending persistent budget deficits, not lifting capital controls. He hopes this approach will advance his political agenda while limiting political tensions and inflation risk.
>
> Milei’s background as a macroeconomist explains his thinking. In this sense, his approach is technocratic because he prioritizes the economic conditions needed to achieve his free-market goals, even if that requires more nuance than his ideological promises.
